newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada border town expects lower Red River crest.
newsitem.headline: Canada border town expects lower Red River crest.

text.p: Displaced residents of towns near the Canada-United States border awoke to the first good news in weeks on Sunday when officials said the Red River's crest may be lower than projected.
The Red was expected to reach its highest level at the mostly evacuated border town of Emerson, Manitoba late Sunday or early Monday.

"There is no change in the forecast for the Red River except at Emerson where the crest will be one foot lower than had been anticipated," Manitoba Natural Resources flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney said.
Thirty nine emergency workers remained behind a massive earthen dike sheltering Emerson, a farming community of 750 people, from the Red River that swelled to 29 km (18 miles) wide Sunday.
Over 17,000 people have been evacuated from southern Manitoba, with many taking refuge in a Winnipeg sports arena.
In what has been called the worst Red River flood since 1852, relentless waters have devastated vast parts of the Dakotas, Minnesota and much of southern Manitoba.
In North Dakota, some people were returning to their homes for a few hours Sunday to begin clean-up efforts but they faced mud everywhere, standing water in basements and the threat of disease.

Officials said 20,000 people in the Grand Forks area had applied for federal assistance so far. No deaths have been attributed directly to the flooding in the area -- the hardest-hit so far -- and police said burglaries and looting had not been a problem even though thousands of structures were left vacant.

Upstream at Fargo, North Dakota, and nearby Moorhead, Minnesota, officials said damage could run as high as $7 million, even though the regions escaped the massive destuction that hit Grand Fork, where unofficial estimates have placed damage at as high as $1 billion.
The Manitoba capital of Winnipeg, a city of 650,000 people, continued a massive effort to shore itself up for the torrent slowly headed its way.
Skies cleared Sunday after half an inch (15 millimetres) of rain fell on southern Manitoba Saturday but more showers are expect Monday, Environment Canada meteorologists said.
If another half-inch of rain falls Monday, provincial engineers would be forced to boost their forecast for flood levels south of Winnipeg, Whitney said.
The rainstorm was forecast to bring winds gusting up to 60 kmh (37 mph), meteorologists said.
Larry Propp, deputy mayor of Emerson, said on Sunday he was confident the dikes surrounding the town would stand up to the Red's highest level, but high winds could pose problems.

"We're in such a huge lake here that we're going to get a lot of wave action that certainly helps to deteriorate the condition of the dikes by wash. But I think we can stand a little bit of that, hopefully it won't keep on for too long," Propp told local radio.
